questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman sought medical advice regarding long-term antibiotic prophylaxis. She was taking benzathine penicillin G every 3 weeks. She had been diagnosed and treated for rheumatic fever when she was 15 years old after developing subcutaneous nodules, polyarthritis, and carditis. Her last echocardiogram showed no residual valvular disease.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue until at least age 40, and possibly lifelong
No indication for any further prophylaxis
Stop prophylaxis but give a rescue box of antibiotics for GAS pharyngitis

questions.explanation: Continue prophylaxis until age 25 All patients with rheumatic fever should receive secondary prophylaxis independent of the presence or absence of carditis and/or residual heart disease; these will only affect the DURATION of prophylaxis. The patient has known RF with carditis but no residual cardiac manifestations. In this case the recommendation is for patients to continue prophylaxis for at least 10 years from diagnosis or until age 21, whichever is longer. Since she was diagnosed at age 15, she should receive prophylaxis until age 25 which is longer than age 21. Short term duration of prophylaxis is only recommended for patients who have RF with no evidence of cardiac involvement. The recommendation to treat until age 40 or lifelong is for patients with RF with carditis and residual valvular disease, which this patient does not have. She has no indication to switch to oral antibiotics, although this could be considered. The success rates of oral prophylaxis at preventing relapse are lower than parenteral prophylaxis even with 100% adherence. Episodes of GAS pharyngitis in the patient or in household contacts should be treated promptly but not at the expense of continuing prophylaxis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q15

parts.text: Name 5 major criteria
Name a minor criterion (symptom)
Name a minor criterion (laboratory)
Name the essential criterion for the diagnosis
Name two prophylactic treatment options when you have confirmed RAA without cardiac involvement

cohort_answer.text:
Five major criteria: Carditis and valvulitis (eg, pancarditis) that is clinical or subclinical; Arthritis (usually migratory polyarthritis predominantly involving the large joints); Sydenham chorea; Subcutaneous nodules; Erythema marginatum
Minor criterion (symptom): Arthralgia (if no arthritis); Fever
Minor criterion (laboratory): Elevated acute phase reactants (ESR/CRP); Prolonged PR interval
Essential criterion: Preceding GAS infection (Positive throat culture for group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, Positive rapid streptococcal antigen test, Elevated or rising antistreptococcal antibody titer)
Diagnosis notes: Two major manifestations or one major plus two minor are sufficient for diagnosis of an initial episode of ARF in a patient with evidence of a preceding GAS infection. Chorea alone is sufficient to dx ARF. Joint (arthritis or arthralgia) and cardiac (carditis or prolonged PR interval) manifestations can only be counted once, not twice, as either a major or a minor criterion. Patients with a history of ARF are at risk of subsequent episodes of ARF with GAS reinfection, and repeat episodes are associated with a greater likelihood of severe cardiac involvement. In these patients, two major, one major plus two minor, or three minor manifestations are sufficient for diagnosis of recurrent ARF.
(No answer documented for two prophylactic treatment options question)

questions.question: A 19-year old male (6-year old child in pediatric exam) is seen for suspected acute rheumatic fever.

parts.text: Name the five major Jones criteria.
Of the minor criteria, name one minor and one laboratory.
For this patient without evidence of cardiac involvement, name two prophylactic regimens and indicate the duration for each.

questions.model_answer: a) Five major Jones criteria: carditis (clinical/subclinical), polyarthritis (or monoarthritis/polyarthralgia in moderate-high risk populations), erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, chorea (Sydenham). b) One minor clinical + one minor laboratory criterion: clinical - fever (≥38.5°C low-risk, ≥38.0°C moderate-high risk) or polyarthralgia/monoarthralgia; laboratory - elevated ESR (≥60 low-risk/≥30 moderate-high risk) or CRP (≥3.0 mg/dL), or prolonged PR interval on ECG. c) Without carditis, secondary prophylaxis (2 regimens with duration): (1) Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million U (600,000 U if ≤27 kg) IM every 4 weeks for 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer. (2) Penicillin V 250 mg PO BID for the same duration (5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer); sulfadiazine or a macrolide are alternatives if penicillin allergic.

questions.question: 9yo girl with sydenham’s chorea.

parts.text: What are 2 risks for recurrence aside from recurrent infx?
What preffered agent for ppx and duration

questions.model_answer: a) Risk factors for chorea recurrence (2, aside from recurrent GAS infection): (1) Pregnancy. (2) Use of oral contraceptives (both can trigger chorea recurrence independent of new streptococcal infection). b) Preferred prophylaxis agent and duration: benzathine penicillin G IM every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks in high-risk settings); duration per ARF-without-carditis category - 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer (chorea alone, without carditis, follows this duration category).

questions.question: You diagnose your 14F patient with Sydenham's chorea – (2019)

parts.text: Other than recurrent GAS infection, what 2 conditions would put her at risk of recurrence?
What is the first line therapy for prophylaxis (please include duration in your answer).

cohort_answer.text: Risk conditions: SLE; Antiphospholipid syndrome. First line prophylaxis: IM pen G benzathine q28days or PenV. Rheumatic fever with carditis and residual heart disease - 10 years or until 40 years of age (sometimes lifelong); Rheumatic fever with carditis but no valvular disease - 10 years or until 21 years of age (whichever longer); Rheumatic fever without carditis - 5 years or 21 years of age (whichever longer)

parts.text: How do you diagnose acute rheumatic fever?
B) What is the treatment for primary and secondary prophylaxis of ARF?

questions.model_answer: a) Diagnosis of ARF (2015 revised Jones criteria): evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (positive throat culture/rapid antigen test or elevated/rising streptococcal antibody titers) PLUS either 2 major manifestations, or 1 major plus 2 minor manifestations (major: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules; minor: fever, arthralgia, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval). b) Primary prophylaxis: treat the antecedent GAS pharyngitis with benzathine penicillin G IM x1 dose (or penicillin V PO x10 days) to prevent first ARF episode. Secondary prophylaxis: benzathine penicillin G IM every 4 weeks (or penicillin V PO BID) for a duration determined by carditis/residual valve disease - 10 years or until age 40 (with residual heart disease), 10 years or until age 21 (carditis without residual disease), or 5 years or until age 21 (no carditis) - whichever is longer in each case.

questions.question: 1. How do you diagnose acute rheumatic fever? [image-based question: image of Erythema Marginatum shown]

parts.text: How do you diagnose acute rheumatic fever?
B) What is the treatment for primary and secondary prophylaxis of ARF?

questions.model_answer: a) Diagnosis of ARF: evidence of antecedent GAS infection plus 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor 2015 revised Jones criteria (major: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum [as shown], subcutaneous nodules; minor: fever, arthralgia, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval). b) Prophylaxis: primary - treat GAS pharyngitis with benzathine penicillin G IM x1 or penicillin V PO x10 days. Secondary - benzathine penicillin G IM every 4 weeks (or oral penicillin V BID), duration based on carditis/valve disease: 10 years or until age 40 if residual heart disease, 10 years or until age 21 if carditis without residual disease, 5 years or until age 21 if no carditis (whichever longer).

questions.question: PM 19. 19 yo patient has rheumatic fever.

parts.text: The 5 major criteria (2.5)
Minor criteria 1 lab and 1 clinical criteria (1)
What must you have to diagnose? (0.5)
Patient is non-carditis, list 2 options for prophylaxis and the duration for each? (2)

cohort_answer.text: Major criteria: Chorea (Sydenham's); Migratory polyarthritis; Erythema marginatum; Subcutaneous nodules; Carditis (subclinical or clinical - echo). Minor criteria: Fever (clinical); Elevated ESR/CRP (lab). Diagnosis requires: Evidence of recent streptococcal infection (culture, positive rapid antigen, or rising ASOT titre). Non-carditis prophylaxis: Penicillin VK 250mg PO BID until age 21 (or 5 years, whichever longer); Benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units IM q3-4 weeks.

parts.text: Name two reasons when this could worsen (besides recurrent GAS)
Prophylaxis (Drug and duration)

cohort_answer.text: Worsening reasons: autoimmunity, damage to the basal ganglia. Prophylaxis: ARF with carditis and residual heart disease - PenG Benzathine q21-28 days x10 years or until age 40 (or lifelong per some sources), whichever longer; ARF with carditis but no residual heart disease - PenG Benzathine q21-28 days x10 years or until age 21, whichever longer; ARF without carditis - PenG Benzathine q21-28 days x5 years or age 21, whichever longer.

questions.question: Man with sore throat 2 wks ago, now comes in with knee arthritis, diagnosed with rheumatic fever.

parts.text: Major diagnostic criteria x 4
Minor diagnostic criteria x 2
What one other criteria is required for diagnosis
Two regimens for secondary prophylaxis in patient without carditis

questions.model_answer: a) Major diagnostic criteria x4 (of the 5): carditis, polyarthritis, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules (chorea is the 5th). b) Minor diagnostic criteria x2: fever and elevated ESR/CRP (prolonged PR interval also acceptable). c) One additional criterion required for diagnosis: evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection (positive throat culture/rapid antigen test, or elevated/rising anti-streptolysin O or anti-DNase B titers). d) Two secondary prophylaxis regimens (no carditis, duration 5 years or until age 21, whichever longer): (1) Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million U IM every 4 weeks. (2) Penicillin V 250 mg PO BID.

questions.question: Rheumatic fever

parts.text: 5 major criteria for diagnosis
1 additional clinical and 1 lab criterion?
1 additional lab needed to make the diagnosis?
How to prophylax if no carditis?

questions.model_answer: a) Five major criteria: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules. b) One additional clinical (minor) and one lab (minor) criterion: clinical - fever (≥38.5°C low-risk/≥38.0°C high-risk) or arthralgia; lab - elevated ESR or CRP. c) One additional lab requirement for diagnosis: evidence of preceding GAS infection (positive throat culture/rapid strep test or elevated/rising ASO or anti-DNase B titers). d) Prophylaxis if no carditis: benzathine penicillin G IM every 4 weeks (or penicillin V PO BID) for 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.

questions.question: 12 year old female from Canada who presents with new mitral valve regurgitation and valve destruction. She had fever and sore throat 1 month ago. You suspect acute rheumatic fever

parts.text: What are the other major Jones criteria besides carditis?
What are the minor Jones criteria you would look for in this case?
She is treated with Amoxicillin. What are two antibiotics you can use for chemoprophylaxis, including medication name and route?

questions.model_answer: a) Other major Jones criteria besides carditis: polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules. b) Minor Jones criteria to look for: fever, arthralgia (if arthritis not used as major), elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval on ECG. c) Two chemoprophylaxis antibiotics (name and route): (1) Benzathine penicillin G, intramuscular, every 4 weeks. (2) Penicillin V, oral, twice daily (or sulfadiazine oral if penicillin allergic without sulfa allergy; macrolide oral if allergic to both).

questions.question: Q48 (2023 Day 1). Describes girl (late teens or early 20s) with rheumatic fever. She was treated with 10 days of amoxicillin. (PEDS)

parts.text: List major JONES criteria aside from carditis
List minor criteria
2 prophylaxis options including drug name and route

cohort_answer.text:
Major JONES criteria (aside from carditis): Arthritis; Chorea; Erythema Marginatum; Subcutaneous nodules.
Minor criteria: Arthralgia (monoarthralgia or polyarthralgia); Fever (≥38°C); ESR >30 and/or CRP >3.0 mg/dL; Prolonged PR interval (unless carditis a major criterion).
2 prophylaxis options: IM Penicillin G Benzathine 1.2 Million units q28 days; Penicillin VK 250mg PO BID; Azithromycin 250mg PO daily.

parts.text: A) 5 major criteria for diagnosis

cohort_answer.text: Jones' criteria: Carditis, Polyarthritis, Chorea, Erythema marginatum, SQ nodules (speaker notes list: Arthritis, carditis, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, sydenham)

parts.text: B) 1 additional clinical and 1 lab criterion

cohort_answer.text: Arthralgia, Fever, Monoarthritis, ESR/CRP, Prolonged PR interval

parts.text: C) 1 additional lab needed to make the diagnosis?
D) How to ppx if no carditis?

cohort_answer.text: 5 years from last episode of ARF OR until age 21. Prophylaxis typically involves an intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin every 4 weeks or oral penicillin V twice daily. Sulfadiazine or oral macrolides for penicillin allergy. Current AHA guidelines no longer recommend bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis for patients with rheumatic heart disease, unless prosthetic valve.
